Reviewer #1:

This is a very nice study of associations between bone fragility, disability, and subsistence costs among a small-scale forager-horticulturalist society, the Tsimane of Bolivia. The study builds on a great recent paper in eLife by the same authors showing that the Tsimane (especially women) have lower average vertebral BMD values than might be expected given their high physical activity levels, as well as surprisingly high rates of vertebral fractures. In this study, they investigate the impact of low vertebral BMD and fracture incidence on disability (or, "adult physical impairment" as they call it) and ultimately the economic costs of such disability. The paper nicely frames the study within evolutionary theory and provides novel insights on the selective pressures that may have shaped human longevity and our species' propensity for age-related fragility. The sample analyzed is impressively large, particularly for a remote-living population like the Tsimane. The CT methods used to collect the bone data are the gold standard. The paper is clear and well written, and the interpretations of the results are all reasonable. Also, the figures are nice. Overall, I think this paper deserves consideration for publication in eLife, but I have a couple of concerns.

First, in my opinion, the possible causal links between bone fragility and disability are not considered or described in enough detail. The only mention of such a link is: "Vertebral deformities are reliably associated with chronic pain…(no citation)" Do the authors have data on back pain? If so, the link between bone fragility and disability would be a lot stronger if they could show that bone fragility is indeed associated with chronic pain among the Tsimane. If not, then it remains possible that bone fragility and disability are only indirectly related. For example, perhaps in many cases bone fragility is just one manifestation of a more general somatic decline, and disability is engendered primarily by other aspects of the general phenomenon and not bone fragility per se. If the authors do not have pain data, I suggest they at least make a stronger argument for the link between bone fragility and pain/disability by citing prior research demonstrating such links.

Second, on the same topic of causal links between bone fragility and disability, I believe the authors must provide a more detailed explanation for how they interpret the contribution of low BMD to disability. Independent of a fracture, there is no clear reason why one would expect low BMD to directly affect disability. Again, it is possible that low BMD and disability could be indirectly related if low BMD is only one of multiple outcomes of general somatic decline. But my understanding is that osteoporosis is generally an asymptomatic disease until fracture occurs. My impression is that the authors may not necessarily be arguing that low BMD, independent of fracture, affects disability, but rather that fracture plus low BMD leads to more disability than a fracture alone. Even so, why does this scenario make sense? Are fractures experienced by a bone with low BMD inherently more painful? Maybe the cooccurrence of fracture and low BMD leads to more disability because such fractures are generally more severe. Or, given that bone fractures can trigger bone loss, maybe the cooccurrence of fractures and low BMD represent cases where fractures took place longer ago and thus potentially have a greater effect on chronic pain and disability. An extreme way of resolving this uncertainty would be for the authors to disregard the BMD data entirely and focus just on the fracture data. The overall storyline would not change too much. However, I am not suggesting the authors do this. The BMD data are potentially important. But the links with disability need to be more carefully considered.

Reviewer #2:

This paper aims to estimate the magnitude of productivity losses associated with compromised bone strength among the Tsimane. The authors specifically test "whether a specific morphological characteristic which may indicate physical impairment, i.e. compromised bone strength, is indeed associated with diminished participation in routine subsistence tasks". They "identify economic correlates of compromised bone strength (i.e. thoracic vertebral body fracture and lower thoracic vertebral BMD) by examining involvement in four common tasks in foraging economies: hunting, tree chopping, tool manufacture (i.e. weaving), and walking long distances".

The data presented in this paper are important and have the potential to make a valuable contribution to the literature, and the authors are to be congratulated for conducing important, unique, and valuable fieldwork. The questions they have posed in this paper are interesting and worthy of consideration. That being said, I have some concerns with the analysis, what it assumes, what it excludes, and the conclusions.

The paper is set to test the "probability of completely ceasing to perform a given task increases with compromised bone strength", and estimate the "magnitude of productivity losses (i.e. lost kcals/day) from hunting cessation associated with compromised bone strength" The authors claim "We do not assume that compromised bone strength is itself a proxy for functional impairment or reduced productivity. Instead we posit that individuals with compromised bone strength who are no longer able to perform specific subsistence tasks facultatively adjust their time allocation based on various factors (e.g. phenotypic condition, household demand) to maximize productivity." This is really unclear and woolly. What, specifically then, are they predicting? If they don't think compromised bone strength influences productivity, why are they testing it, and why is the text replete with indications that they are interpreting this as a direct influence?

The authors make their assumptions of the direction of this relationship clear throughout the paper, through the use of language such as "To estimate men's hunting productivity losses associated with fracture and lower BMD". The paper is replete with the inference of this relationship, and while the authors might carefully choose their words in places to try to avoid causation, the inference is there for the reader to make. Perhaps another way of putting this is the following: the authors show correlations between measures of later life activity/productivity and both increase fracture prevalence and lower BMD. There are three parsimonious explanations for this correlation:

1) The loss of bone quality is the cause of a decline in involvement in economic activity

2) The loss of bone quality is correlated with age, which independently corresponds with later life declines in economic activity, and the two are not directly related but collinear

3) A later life decline in activity is the cause of a decline in bone quality.

These are simplistic explanations, and there are likely other factors involved (see comments below), but for the purposes of simplicity, let's consider the above. The language of the paper is only oriented around the first explanation and the direction of causality is assumed through most of the text, but only really directly acknowledged when they briefly address the possibility of “reverse causality” (reductions in activity causing a reduction in bone strength). They attempt to test for “reverse causality” through indirect methods: comparing fracture status to self-reported reasons for task cessation, and the use of GLM to compare BMD of those who cease versus those who continue participation. I'm not convinced that these adequately address the challenges of the direction of the relationship. Self-reported causes may, in some cases, related to injury (particularly in severe cases), but are much more likely to relate to other factors entirely, and to be unrelated to BMD. The GLM comparisons of BMD among groups defined by continued participation in activity may be influenced by study design, and I am not certain it is testing the reverse causation that the authors suggest. The most significant influence on later life bone mass is earlier life activity. Peak bone mass is commonly achieved between the ages of 20 and 30, and is the single most important predictor of later life bone mass. The more you build early on, the more bone you have to lose. Activity at age 20 may thus be stronger correlate of bone mass after the age of 40 than recent activity patterns. It is curious that the authors point out that "Physical strength peaks in the mid to late 20s, then declines continuously thereafter, reaching ~60% of maximum adult capacity by age 70 (Gurven et al., 2006)." This is essentially the same trajectory of bone strength acquisition and loss, and there is considerable evidence that bone strength corresponds with muscle induced loads. One could argue the most parsimonious explanation is that the most active and economically productive individuals during young adulthood have the highest peak bone mass, and are more likely to remain productive (or with higher than average productivity) later in life.

Apart from the issues noted above, I remain sceptical about causation. There is, in theory, a direct causal relationship between fractures and decline or cessation of economic activity. This is supported by the relatively strong results, for example, the declines in weaving and ability to walk for a day associated with earlier fractures. What is the causal mechanism for the relationship with BMD? Going back to the three possible interpretations I mentioned earlier, I would have no issue with the statement of a hypothesis that vertebral fracture is the cause of a decline in involvement in economic activity. If I were to hypothesize what would explain the correspondence with BMD, I would go for a variant of the second hypothesis, that it is correlated with age, which independently correlates with other measures that are associated with later life declines. There are multiple collinear biological trends associated with senescence. While the authors provide no consideration of a biological mechanism through which BMD would be associated directly with productivity, the inference of causation is made without consideration of the particular relationship of declines in BMD associated with other factors of aging.

I am also sceptical of the consideration of both BMD and trauma as indicators of bone strength. BMD is highly correlated with bone mechanical function, this is uncontroversial, but considering trauma as a similar indicator may be problematic. Demographers and epidemiologists have often noted that trauma occurs in different societies with a relatively consistent frequency (at least when compared to infectious or metabolic disease, for example), because they result from accidental injury which tend to occur with some statistical regularity in larger populations. The data in Figure 2 suggest that there is no real difference the relationship between BMD and Age between groups of men with and without fracture, which could be interpreted as evidence that fracture prevalence among is predominantly determined by accidents rather than a loss of bone strength, regardless of the age or BMD of the individual. In contrast, there appear to be considerable differences among the women measured, suggesting that BMD and Fractures are more strongly correlated in women. The male data, at least, would seem to contradict the assertion that fracture prevalence is a proxy for bone strength.

results.result: The study reports thoracic vertebral fracture prevalence among Tsimane adults aged 40+. For men, 36% have grade ≥1 fractures and 11% have grade ≥2 fractures, with neither age nor BMD significantly associated with fracture risk. For women, 19% have grade 1 fractures and 7% have grade 2 fractures, with BMD inversely associated with fracture risk after adjusting for age.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C60 present descriptive epidemiological findings with confidence intervals and statistical tests. The data are derived from CT imaging of a representative sample (n=493) using validated methods (Genant's semi-quantitative technique). The sex-specific differences in BMD-fracture associations are clearly documented with appropriate statistical adjustments.

results.result: Thoracic vertebral fracture is strongly associated with hunting cessation among Tsimane men. After adjusting for age, men with fracture have 7.3 times greater odds of ceasing hunting compared to men without fracture (p<0.001). The productivity impact varies by age, with younger men showing smaller deficits due to high baseline hunting participation regardless of fracture status.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C61-C63 are supported by statistical analysis with appropriate controls (age adjustment), multiple testing correction (FDR), and clear effect sizes (OR=7.3, 95% CI: 3.3-17.6). The age-stratified analysis (Table 1) provides additional context showing the differential impact across age groups.

results.result: Thoracic vertebral fracture is strongly associated with tree chopping cessation among Tsimane men. After adjusting for age, men with fracture have 6.9 times greater odds of ceasing tree chopping compared to men without fracture (p<0.001).
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C76-C77 are supported by statistical analysis with appropriate controls and multiple testing correction. The effect size (OR=6.9, 95% CI: 3.1-16.6) is comparable to that for hunting cessation, suggesting consistent impact of fracture on high-strength activities.

results.result: Thoracic vertebral fracture is not significantly associated with weaving cessation among Tsimane women. After adjusting for age, the odds ratio for weaving cessation is 2.2 (95% CI: 0.8-6.4, p=0.129), making weaving the only examined task where fracture does not significantly compromise participation.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C78-C80 are supported by statistical analysis showing non-significant associations. The contrast with other tasks (hunting, tree chopping, walking) strengthens the interpretation that fracture selectively impacts high-strength/endurance activities. However, the wide confidence interval suggests limited statistical power for this analysis.

results.result: Thoracic vertebral fracture is strongly associated with inability to walk all day among Tsimane adults. After adjusting for age and sex, adults with fracture have 8.2 times greater odds of being unable to walk all day compared to those without fracture (p<0.001).
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C81-C82 are supported by statistical analysis with appropriate controls for both age and sex. The effect size (OR=8.2, 95% CI: 4.8-14.5) is the largest among all examined activities, suggesting walking endurance is particularly compromised by fracture.

results.result: Hunting cessation associated with fracture generates substantial daily productivity losses for Tsimane men. At age 61, men with fracture produce 481 fewer hunting kcals/day than men without fracture, representing 19% of mean daily energy intake and 52% of protein/fat intake. These losses exceed daily fishing production by 171 kcals and would require 51-76 additional minutes of fishing per day to offset. Average losses from ages 40-74 are 261 kcals/day.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C64-C69, C92 present quantitative productivity estimates based on combining fracture-hunting associations with previously published age-specific production data. The calculations are transparent and appropriately contextualized relative to dietary needs and alternative food sources (fishing). However, the estimates assume identical hunting efficiency (kcals/hr) regardless of fracture status, which may underestimate true losses.

results.result: Expected cumulative future hunting productivity losses associated with fracture are substantial. At age 40, men with fracture can expect to lose 1.15 million kcals over their remaining life, representing 14% of total future hunting production. These losses exceed future fishing productivity for 16 years (ages 49-64), requiring 324-2347 additional future fishing days to offset.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8, C70-C72 extend the daily productivity analysis to lifetime estimates by incorporating mortality discounting. The approach is conceptually sound (analogous to reproductive value calculations) and provides important context for understanding long-term economic impacts. However, the estimates assume stable fracture-productivity relationships over time and do not account for potential behavioral adaptations.

results.result: Productivity losses are greatest for men with both fracture and lower BMD compared to men without fracture and higher BMD. Average losses are 397 kcals/day (15% of daily energy intake, 44% of protein/fat intake), with peak losses of 650 kcals/day at age 60 (25% of daily energy intake, 70% of protein/fat intake).
results.evaluation: Claims C93, C73-C75 extend the fracture-only analysis to include BMD effects. The combined analysis shows additive effects of fracture and low BMD on productivity losses. The calculations follow the same methodology as the fracture-only analysis and are appropriately presented with contextual comparisons to dietary needs.

results.result: Men with fracture are more likely to report mobility limitations due to hip problems as reasons for hunting and tree chopping cessation. Notably, among men who ceased these activities, those with fracture are younger on average than those without fracture (mean ages 63 vs. 68 for hunting; 62 vs. 68 for tree chopping).
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C84 provide suggestive evidence that fracture precedes task cessation rather than the reverse. The age differential strengthens this interpretation, as younger men with fracture reporting mobility problems suggests fracture-related disability rather than general age-related decline. However, this remains correlational evidence and cannot definitively establish temporal ordering.

results.result: Among Tsimane women, thoracic vertebral body BMD is inversely associated with fracture risk after adjusting for age, with relative risks of 0.49 (grade 1) and 0.25 (grade 2) per SD increase in BMD.
results.evaluation: Claims C89 and C60 are supported by statistical analysis showing significant inverse associations between BMD and fracture risk in women. The effect sizes are substantial and biologically plausible, suggesting compromised bone strength contributes to fracture risk in this population.

results.result: The study sample includes 493 Tsimane adults aged 40+ (mean age 55.9±9.9 years, 48% female) who underwent thoracic CT scanning. This sample is thought to be representative of all Tsimane aged 40+.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C49 describe the study sample. The sample size is adequate and the age/sex distribution is clearly reported. The assertion of representativeness is stated but not empirically validated in the manuscript, though the authors reference prior work suggesting representativeness.

results.result: The study uses validated CT-based methods for measuring bone mineral density and fracture. CT-derived BMD estimates correlate strongly (r>0.9) with ash weight and lumbar BMD. Phantomless estimates correlate strongly (r=0.99) with phantom-based estimates. Genant's semi-quantitative technique provides highly reproducible fracture diagnosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C53 describe methodological validation based on prior published research. The cited correlations support the validity of the measurement approaches used in this study. These are appropriate methodological citations establishing measurement validity.

results.result: Bone mineral density accounts for approximately 70% of the variance in bone strength.
results.evaluation: Claim C28 is supported by citation to an NIH consensus panel. This is an established finding in bone biology that provides rationale for using BMD as a proxy for bone strength in this study.

results.result: The manuscript provides extensive descriptive information about the Tsimane population, including their subsistence patterns, physical activity levels, age-related changes in strength and activity, and prevalence of musculoskeletal conditions. Key findings include: men hunt every 1-2 weeks with hunts lasting 8.4 hours and covering 17.9 km; 62% of calories come from cultigens; physical strength peaks in the mid-to-late 20s and declines to ~60% of maximum by age 70; thoracic vertebral fracture prevalence is 2-3.3 times higher than US controls; 38% of adults 50+ experience movement restrictions; and 70% have diagnosed musculoskeletal conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C47 provide population context supported by citations to prior research and descriptive data from the current study. These claims establish the study population characteristics and justify the focus on this population for understanding disability-productivity relationships. The claims are well-documented but primarily serve as background rather than novel findings.

results.result: Tsimane thoracic vertebral fractures appear to result from both trauma and senescence and are not just prevalent among the oldest adults, as shown in Figures 2 and 3.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C88 are supported by citation to prior work and visual evidence in the figures showing fracture distribution across age groups. The figures show fractures occurring across the age range studied (40-91 years), not just in the oldest individuals.

results.result: High reproductive effort is associated with reduced bone strength for Tsimane women, and intimate partner violence is prevalent, particularly among younger women, potentially precipitating traumatic fractures.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C91 are supported by citations to prior research on this population. These claims provide context for understanding potential mechanisms underlying women's fracture risk but are not directly tested in the current study.

results.result: Trabecular bone losses during adulthood are not fully regained, and spinal fracture may impede daily subsistence activities for the remainder of life once it occurs.
results.evaluation: Claim C85 is supported by citations to prior research on bone biology. Claim C86 is a speculative statement about long-term consequences that is plausible given C85 but not directly tested in this study. The speculation is reasonable but should be clearly identified as such.

results.result: For comparison, adults in Western industrialized settings with musculoskeletal problems show productivity losses of 10-15% for computer users, up to 28% for construction workers, and costs exceeding 25% of mean annual income for osteoporotic adults with spine fractures in the Netherlands.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C96 provide comparative context from other populations based on cited research. These comparisons help contextualize the magnitude of productivity losses observed among the Tsimane, though direct comparisons are limited by differences in work types and measurement approaches.

results.result: Tsimane age-specific energetic deficits peak in the early 60s, which is near the age at which Tsimane adults achieve peak numbers of dependent offspring and grand offspring.
results.evaluation: Claim C97 is supported by the productivity calculations shown in Figures 4 and 5. Claim C98 is supported by citation to prior research. Together, these claims highlight the potential fitness consequences of disability-related productivity losses occurring at ages when dependency loads are highest.

results.result: Aging women may maintain peak subsistence involvement with minimal disability-related productivity losses despite increasing frailty, given the sexual division of labor where men focus on high-strength tasks. In industrialized populations, severe thoracolumbar vertebral deformity is more strongly associated with functional impairments for men than women, perhaps because men load their spines more heavily.
results.evaluation: Claim C99 is an inference from the study findings showing fracture does not significantly impact weaving (a female task) but does impact hunting and tree chopping (male tasks). Claim C100 is supported by citation to prior research. Claim C101 is a speculative explanation that is plausible but not directly tested.

results.result: Fishing is an important source of protein and fat for Tsimane. Tsimane cognitive function is generally well preserved throughout adulthood, consistent with a late-life service niche emphasizing information transmission.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C104 are supported by citations to prior research. These claims provide context for understanding potential compensatory strategies (fishing) and alternative contributions (knowledge transmission) for adults with compromised physical abilities.

results.result: Extant hunter-gatherers exhibit a modal adult lifespan of 68-78 years. Extensive longevity may be a novel feature of modern H. sapiens absent in prior hominin species. The study's estimates of disability-related productivity loss may be more relevant for understanding past hominin populations with life histories similar to modern H. sapiens.
results.evaluation: Claim C105 is supported by citation to prior research. Claims C106-C107 are speculative statements about the generalizability of findings to past populations. The speculation is appropriately cautious and acknowledges limitations in extrapolating to hominins with different life histories.

results.result: Ache hunters cite fear of disability as an important reason for conforming to food sharing conventions. Individuals may have survived prolonged disability only via costly provisioning by others.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C109 are supported by citations to prior research on other populations. These claims provide comparative context for understanding the social implications of disability-related productivity losses, though the extent of compensatory provisioning is noted as beyond the scope of the current study.

results.result: The manuscript presents evolutionary and comparative context for understanding human disability. Key points include: humans experience unique physical impairments with potentially large consequences; human hunter-gatherers have lower adult mortality than chimpanzees and significant post-reproductive lifespans, generating opportunity for degenerative disease; hominins showed greater dietary reliance on difficult-to-acquire resources at least 2 million years ago, suggesting delayed peak skill acquisition possibly when senescence was underway; and hunter-gatherers form multi-generational resource-pooling units, possibly reflecting cooperative strategies to minimize risks including production shortfalls.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C9-C18 provide evolutionary and anthropological context supported by citations to prior research. These claims establish the theoretical framework and rationale for the study but are not novel findings. Some claims (C14, C15, C18) involve speculation that is appropriately identified as such.

results.result: Skeletal evidence shows thoracic kyphosis and vertebral disc degeneration in Australopithecus afarensis (~3.2 mya) and spondylolisthesis in middle Pleistocene humans (~430 kya). These ailments regularly cause lower back pain, difficulty walking, and carrying/lifting problems in modern clinical patients, who may provide indirect insights into consequences of disability in past hominin populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C21 are supported by citations to prior research. Claim C22 is a speculative inference about using modern clinical data to understand past populations. The speculation is reasonable but appropriately identified as providing only indirect insights.

results.result: Prior studies of small-scale subsistence populations show substantial disability burdens: Yora men unable to forage 11% of days; >60% of Shiwiar experience impairments interfering with subsistence work ≥1 month, with fractures particularly likely to cause prolonged disability; 75% of Tsimane report being bedridden at least once in 3 months, and Tsimane are incapacitated ~10% of days.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C27 are supported by citations to prior research. These claims establish that disability is common in subsistence populations and provide comparative context for the current study's findings.

results.result: Thoracic vertebral deformity is regularly observed in diverse hominin skeletal samples. Thoracic vertebral fractures are among the most common fragility fractures in post-industrialized populations and are more common among Tsimane than US controls. Spontaneous vertebral fractures have not been observed in other great apes, even with severe osteopenia, suggesting bipedal hominins are especially susceptible to spinal fragility fractures.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C33 are supported by citations to prior research. These claims establish the prevalence and evolutionary context of vertebral fractures, providing rationale for focusing on this skeletal site in the current study.

results.result: Most activities of daily living generate vertebral loads, and for many common activities the greatest spinal compressive loads are generated in the thoracolumbar region.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C35 are supported by citations to prior biomechanical research. These claims provide rationale for expecting thoracic vertebral fractures to impact a wide range of subsistence activities.

results.result: Vertebral deformities are observed in diverse hominin skeletal samples, yet their social and behavioral implications remain obscure. Bone properties may represent a potential proxy for inferring behavioral consequences of skeletal deformity in prior hominin populations.
